title: tand
summary: Compute element-wise tangent values for degree-based angles with MATLAB-compatible canonical handling.

gpu_support.notes: GPU inputs use an owner-preserving host fallback so canonical degree values and poles match the reference implementation while the result returns to the source provider when its precision is compatible.

fusion.notes: Fusion is intentionally disabled for v1 because the WGSL `tan(x*pi/180)` form would replace MATLAB's +/-Inf poles with very large but finite values.

description: `y = tand(x)` computes tangent using degree-based angles rather than radians. It follows MATLAB-compatible canonical handling for key multiples, including exact zeros at 180-degree multiples and poles at odd 90-degree multiples.
behaviors: Operates element-wise on scalars, vectors, matrices, and N-D tensors.
Documented single inputs return single and documented double inputs return double.

Typed integers and logical inputs are independently gated RunMat extensions. Integer angles are reduced exactly modulo 360 before floating evaluation, so wide int64 and uint64 inputs are never rounded through a double angle mirror.
Returns exactly 0 at multiples of 180 and exactly ±1 at multiples of 45.
Returns +Inf at +90 (and angles equivalent under modulo 360) and -Inf at -90 (and equivalent angles).
Complex inputs delegate to the analytic extension of `tan` after scaling by `pi/180`; exact-value treatment for complex operands is deferred.
Output shape matches the input shape; non-finite inputs propagate as `NaN`.
String inputs are unsupported and raise a builtin-scoped error. MATLAB's documented direct table and timetable calculation form is not implemented yet.

examples.description: Tangent of a canonical degree angle
Tangent of a multiple of 180 returns exactly zero

faqs.question: Why does `tand(90)` return Inf instead of a very large finite number?
faqs.answer: MATLAB defines `tand(90) = Inf` and `tand(-90) = -Inf` at the poles. Naively evaluating `tan(90*pi/180)` would return a huge finite number because `pi/180` is not exact in floating point, so RunMat short-circuits the poles to match MATLAB.

faqs.question: Is `tand(x)` equivalent to `tan(x*pi/180)`?
faqs.answer: Mathematically yes, but the floating-point result differs at canonical angles. `tand` guarantees exact values at multiples of 45 and 180, and infinite values at +/-90.

faqs.question: Does `tand` support arrays?
faqs.answer: Yes. Scalars, vectors, matrices, and N-D tensors are all handled element-wise; the shape of the input is preserved.
